Cuba is not a resort. It is a living culture.

Travel with us to engage with Cuban families, artists and communities, not to consume a packaged holiday. We are transparent about the realities of travel in Cuba today: the power cuts, the fuel, the paperwork. We think that honesty is the beginning of trust, and the beginning of a better trip.

Vereda means "path" in Spanish: the narrow track between farms, the one locals use. We are a small Spanish-registered agency with an operations desk in Havana, a network of licensed casas, drivers and guides we know by name, and no interest in state hotel chains.
alt: Ana and host Lis on a Vedado balcony
The total price before you click. The power schedule before you book. The 3-star review next to the 5-star one. Where every euro goes, on the invoice.
85 % or more of what you spend reaches Cuban families: casas, paladares, farms, guides and drivers. Guides keep their whole day rate. We publish the split per trip.
Named hosts, named villages, named traditions. "Bring € 300–500 in cash", not "bring sufficient cash". We say what we mean and we date it.
Built around people, because Cuban hosts don't have booking APIs

Every casa is visited by our Havana team: licence, backup power (generator, battery or solar), 24 h water storage, a host who answers within 30 minutes, a walk to the plaza of 15 minutes or less. Drivers hold a transport licence and a vehicle we've sat in. Guides are Formatur-certified.

Your request goes to each host's phone. They answer within 24 hours, you watch it happen, and nothing is charged until all of them have said yes. If one is full, we propose up to three alternatives at the same price.

A Reality Briefing 30 days out, reconfirmation at 7 days and 48 hours, a WhatsApp check-in every morning in Cuba, and a phone line that answers in 15 minutes, day or night. If a storm or a blackout breaks the plan, we rebook, refund or relocate, and we say which within the hour.

Twenty-hour apagones are the baseline this year, not the exception. Here's what a cut looks like from inside a casa, what a generator does and doesn't run, and the four things we do before you arrive.
Published 14 Feb 2026 · Updated 1 Oct 2026 · next review Nov 2026
alt: Candle, power bank and coffee on a casa table during an evening apagón, Viñales
Evening at Casa Yamilé during a scheduled cut. The generator runs the fridge and fans; the candle is for atmosphere. Photo: Vereda, with permission.
What we do before you arrive
Pinar del Río: 6–10 h cuts. Havana: 4–8 h.

Cuba's power plants are old, fuel is short, and demand peaks in the evening when everyone cooks. The national utility publishes a daily deficit and provinces take turns going dark. In 2025 the island had several total blackouts lasting more than a day; in 2026 planned cuts of 12 to 20 hours outside Havana are normal in the hot months.
None of this is a secret in Cuba. Your hosts plan their day around it: cooking early, charging phones when the light is on, keeping a torch by the bed. You will too, and it is easier than it sounds.
What a cut looks like from inside a casa

Usually the schedule is known a day ahead; Yamilé will tell you at breakfast that the light goes at four. The fan stops, the fridge hums off, and the street gets quieter. If the casa has a generator it starts within a minute and the essentials come back. If it has a battery, the lights and the Wi-Fi router stay on but the air conditioning doesn't.

Evenings are the hardest part: it is hot, and there is less to do. Our travelers' tip, repeated in every review that mentions outages, is to be out. Dinner at a paladar with its own generator, music at the Casa de la Música, a walk along the Malecón. The casa is for sleeping, and a fan on a generator is enough for that.
"Two nights without power, ten hours each. The generator kept the fan on and Ana messaged every morning. Honest, tiring, worth it. Knowing in advance is what made it OK."
Marion T., Lyon · Viñales, February 2026 · verified review
What a generator does and doesn't run
lights, fans, the fridge, phone charging, the router. Usually for 4 to 8 hours a night; fuel for generators is also rationed.
air conditioning in most casas, electric showers, kettles. Premium stays with 24-hour generators are the exception and cost accordingly.
quieter, no fuel, but smaller. Good for lights, charging and the router for 6 to 8 hours.
most casas use tanks heated when the grid is up. Shower early.

Because the outage is also when the street comes alive: neighbours on the porch, dominoes under a single bulb on a battery, someone with a guitar. We won't romanticise it, Cubans don't, and it is a real hardship for the people who live with it every day. But if you understand the reality before you go, you can handle the inconvenience, and what you can't handle is being surprised. A valley of limestone mogotes where tobacco is still planted by hand and ox. You stay with families in the village, walk the red-earth tracks with a biologist, and learn how a leaf becomes a cigar from the people who grow it, not from a shop.

The valley is a UNESCO cultural landscape and a working farm district of about 28,000 people. The village has one main street, a church square and a few hundred licensed casas; the valley has farms, caves and birds. Days are slow and early; nights are dark when the grid is down, and the stars are the compensation.

It is not a resort and not a theme park. Horse rides and farm visits are run by families who also farm; prices are set with them, and tipping the farmer directly is normal. Expect mud in the rainy season and dust in the dry one.

What we do before you arrive

Cuba's power plants are old, fuel is short, and demand peaks in the evening. The utility publishes a daily deficit and provinces take turns going dark. In 2026 planned cuts of 12 to 20 hours outside Havana are normal in the hot months.
Your hosts plan their day around it: cooking early, charging phones when the light is on, a torch by the bed. You will too, and it is easier than it sounds.
What a cut looks like from inside a casa

The schedule is usually known a day ahead. The fan stops, the fridge hums off, the street gets quieter. A generator starts within a minute and the essentials come back; a battery keeps lights and the router but not the air conditioning.

Evenings are the hard part. Our travelers' tip: be out. Dinner at a paladar with its own generator, music, a walk on the Malecón. The casa is for sleeping, and a fan on a generator is enough for that.

Under the Cuban Assets Control Regulations, US persons may only spend money on Cuba travel under one of 12 general-licence categories, whatever the booking channel or payment method. Tourism as such is not one of them. Vereda is a Spanish company; the rules still apply to you.

: a full-time schedule of activities with private hosts, farmers, artists and guides, avoiding restricted state entities. Family visits, journalism, professional research, religious and humanitarian work are others. As of 30 Sep 2026 the people-to-people group category no longer exists.
A short form before payment: category, your name as on the passport, a typed signature. We store it for 5 years as the law requires and give you a PDF.
Your itinerary is the schedule. Keep it, your receipts and your voucher for 5 years. We don't book GAESA or Gaviota properties, nor anything on the US restricted list.

US-issued cards are declined by our gateway. Pay by international wire or invoice. No transaction is cleared in US dollars.

"Family visits" covers close relatives in Cuba. Our Family Visit package is built for it: airport transfers, a casa near your family, luggage for supplies, Spanish-speaking desk. Remittance and gift rules are separate; ask us.
